The post WEEKEND READING: Universities do not lack opportunity. They lose it in the flow appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr John Milliken, a retired academic from Queen’s University Belfast, University of Ulster & the Open University.

Universities are frequently criticised for failing to prepare students adequately for employment, respond quickly enough to employers or contribute visibly enough to regional growth. The usual response is to call for more partnerships, more placements, more employer engagement, more entrepreneurship and more civic activity.

Yet many universities already undertake all these things.

The deeper problem is not necessarily the absence of activity. It is the failure to connect activity into a coherent process.

Universities generate knowledge, educate students, undertake research, work with employers, support innovation, engage with communities and maintain relationships with graduates. But these functions are often organised as separate institutional territories. Careers teams gather employer intelligence that may never reach programme designers. Researchers develop knowledge that may not reach local businesses. Alumni accumulate decades of professional experience but remain largely disconnected from current students. Employers contribute to advisory panels without seeing whether their advice influences decisions. Students complete placements, projects and dissertations whose learning is rarely captured systematically by the institution.

The university is therefore busy, but not always flowing. This distinction matters. Activity can be counted. Flow must be traced.

A flow-based university would examine how opportunity moves through the institution:

Observation → Information → Interpretation → Decision → Action → Outcome → Learning

The process begins with observation. Universities must remain attentive to changes in employment, technology, communities, professions and society. Signals may emerge from employers, students, graduates, professional bodies, research, public services or local communities.

Observation alone, however, achieves little. What is noticed must become information. That information must be gathered, tested and shared rather than remaining within one department, committee or professional service.

Information must then be interpreted. A shortage of particular skills, for example, may not require a new degree programme. It may require changes to existing modules, short professional courses, workplace learning, conversion provision or collaboration with further education. Interpretation prevents institutions from responding to every external demand with the same familiar solution.

Interpretation must lead to decision. This is often where flow slows or stops. Universities are highly capable of establishing working groups, consultation exercises and steering committees. They are sometimes less effective at identifying who has the authority to decide, what evidence is required and when action should begin.

Decision must then become action. Curriculum changes must reach students. Research partnerships must generate application. Employer engagement must produce meaningful experience rather than ceremonial association. Enterprise support must help ideas progress beyond competitions, presentations and photographs.

Action must produce an outcome that can be examined. Did students gain stronger employment prospects? Did an employer solve a genuine problem? Did a new course meet an identified need? Did research improve practice? Did a community receive lasting benefit?

Finally, outcomes must generate learning. Without this final stage, institutions repeatedly launch initiatives without accumulating institutional wisdom. Successful projects remain isolated, while failed projects quietly disappear and are later reinvented under new names.

This is why universities do not always need more initiatives. They need greater integrity in the movement between existing ones.

The student journey is also a flow process

The same principle applies to students. The student journey is often presented as a sequence beginning with recruitment and ending with graduation. This creates an artificial boundary. Graduation should not be regarded as the completion of the university’s interest in a student, but as a transition into another stage of development.

Students enter university with prior knowledge, employment, family responsibilities, cultural experience and personal capabilities. These should flow into the learning process rather than being treated as irrelevant background. During study, academic knowledge should flow into application through placements, projects, simulation, enterprise and workplace learning. Experience gained outside the classroom should then flow back into reflection, discussion and assessment.

After graduation, professional experience should continue to flow back into the university. Graduates can become mentors, guest contributors, placement providers, research partners and sources of intelligence about changing workplaces. They should not simply be recorded as employment outcomes and contacted when the institution requires donations.

A healthy university relationship is cyclical rather than terminal.

Experience must move in both directions

Universities also need to reconsider the movement of professional experience. Too often, the relationship between higher education and employment is imagined as a one-way process: universities prepare students and employers receive them. In reality, knowledge should travel in both directions.

Practitioners should contribute to teaching. Academic staff should remain connected to professional practice. Employers should help identify emerging needs. Students should bring current workplace problems into learning. Researchers should translate findings into forms that practitioners can use. Retired professionals and academics should not disappear from the system when they leave formal employment; they represent an enormous reserve of experience, judgment and institutional memory.

The question is not simply whether these people are connected to the university. It is whether their knowledge can move to where it is needed.

Universities often possess more expertise than they recognise because it is held in separate departments, professional services, partnerships, alumni communities and individual careers. Flow makes that expertise visible and usable.

Partnership without flow is largely ceremonial

The language of partnership is now embedded throughout higher education. Universities partner with employers, colleges, schools, public services, local authorities and community organisations.

But the existence of a partnership does not demonstrate its value. A partnership should be judged by what passes through it. Does information move? Are problems jointly interpreted? Are decisions changed? Are resources committed? Does action occur? Are outcomes evaluated? Does learning return to all participants?

Where these stages are absent, partnership can become ceremonial. Meetings are held, agreements are signed and newsletters are produced, but the underlying systems remain unchanged. A flow approach would therefore replace the question, “Who are our partners?” with a more demanding one:What moves between us, where does it go and what changes as a result?

Leadership must protect the whole pathway

Universities are traditionally organised through faculties, schools, departments and professional services. These structures provide expertise, accountability and identity. They should not simply be swept away in the name of integration. But every structure creates boundaries, and every boundary creates the possibility that information or responsibility will stop.

Leadership must therefore protect the integrity of the whole pathway. This means identifying where flow breaks down between observation and information, between evidence and decision, between decision and action, or between outcome and learning.

It also means rewarding contribution across boundaries. A member of staff who connects students with employers, translates research into practice or brings professional knowledge into the curriculum may create substantial value without fitting neatly into conventional measures of teaching or research performance.

The flow university would recognise the people who carry ideas across the institution, not only those who generate them within a particular part of it.

From institutional activity to institutional movement

The future of higher education will not be secured merely by adding more programmes, strategies, partnerships or committees. Universities already contain remarkable concentrations of knowledge, talent and possibility. Their challenge is to make these resources move.

A university creates opportunity when observation becomes information, information becomes understanding, understanding becomes decision, decision becomes action, action creates value and experience improves what happens next.

Where that flow is intact, teaching, research, enterprise and civic engagement reinforce one another. Where it is broken, opportunity is not necessarily absent. It is simply lost somewhere inside the institution.

Universities do not need to behave like graduate factories. Nor should they define themselves through a collection of separate missions. They should become integrated systems through which knowledge, experience and opportunity can flow.

title: ‘Our children are less cognitively capable,’ says neuroscientist who wants to cut screen use in schools
summary:
Jared Cooney Horvath argues that educational technology undermines how children learn and develop

Jared Cooney Horvath is on a mission. In the wake of global campaigns for smartphone bans in schools and social media restrictions for under-16s, the neuroscientist wants to raise the alarm about educational technology in classrooms.

A former teacher, Horvath believes the use of screens and digital tools in schools is undermining how children learn and develop. “This might be one of the hardest truths our generation has to face,” he writes in his book, The Digital Delusion.

full_text:
Jared Cooney Horvath is on a mission. In the wake of global campaigns for smartphone bans in schools and social media restrictions for under-16s, the neuroscientist wants to raise the alarm about educational technology in classrooms.

A former teacher, Horvath believes the use of screens and digital tools in schools is undermining how children learn and develop. “This might be one of the hardest truths our generation has to face,” he writes in his book, The Digital Delusion.

“Our children are less cognitively capable than we were at their age,” he says. “For nearly two centuries, the west experienced steady generational progress. Each new cohort of children grew up, on average, healthier, happier, and better educated than the last. Until now.”

Starting around the year 2000, something changed. “Across the west, IQ scores began to fall – even as time spent in school kept rising,” writes Horvath. Scores in international tests started to drop. Why? “The answer lies in the meteoric rise of educational technology.”

According to a recent Department for Education report, the UK educational technology – or edtech – market generated an annual turnover of about £6.5bn. In the US, Horvath says it is a $400bn (£295bn) mega-industry, woven into every aspect of schooling.

“We’ve been making some incredible strides on the screen-based childhood stuff which even two years ago, I did not think was going to happen as fast as it did,” he said. “But it’s not just about getting rid of screens for entertainment. It’s about reducing them as much as possible for academic learning as well if we want our kids to have deep transferrable knowledge in our heads.”

The uptake of laptops in schools – especially in the US where he lives – began in earnest in 2010-12, Horvath said. “It’s when Covid hit, that’s when every school had to pivot digital as a Band-Aid … rightly so. Better to have something than nothing.

“But when Covid finished you would assume they’d rip that Band-Aid off, but the vast majority of schools didn’t. They just stayed digital.” In the US 88% of school districts now had one-to-one computers, he said. In the UK, Covid had a similar impact.

Horvath has been studying how people learn for over 15 years and has concluded that “tech is not a very good tool for it”. He cites recent scores from the programme for international student assessment (Pisa) which takes place every three years and tracks the academic performance of 15-year-olds across dozens of countries.

In 2012, 2015 and 2018, Pisa asked students how much time they spent using digital devices during a typical school day. “The more time students spent on screens at school, the further their scores fell,” Horvath said. “On average, those who used computers for more than six hours per day scored 66 points lower than their peers who didn’t use them at all.”

Others working in the field are concerned about the risks of confusing correlation with causation. Rose Luckin is an emerita professor of learner-centred design at the UCL Knowledge Lab in London and a recognised expert on AI in education.

“[Horvath] does get certain things right,” Luckin said. “It’s true that a great deal of educational technology was sold on promises rather than proof. We did not have a huge amount of evidence. But that does not mean that all educational technology is problematic.

“In terms of that Pisa data, if you look at it on computer use and outcomes, actually moderate school device use is associated with better results than no school device use. It’s just that the heaviest daily use is the worst.”

Daisy Christodoulou, the director of education at No More Marking, an educational technology startup, agrees that society has been a “bit blase” about the impact of a lot of these new technologies.

“We are seeing across the board now a bit of a corrective, where people are realising that. But I would probably be a little bit more optimistic [than Horvath] about the potential for technology and AI in upper secondary,” she said. “Screens have not had as big an impact in classrooms in England as in the US. But I feel like there’s enough here that we should be thinking about it. I think it’s a bit blase to go, ‘nothing to see here’, move on please’.”

Dylan Wiliam, an emeritus professor of educational assessment at the UCL Institute of Education, said: “Technology may well be harming student achievement but the correlational studies that we currently have cannot support such causal claims.

“And there are many well-designed studies that show that technology can have a positive impact on student achievement. So the question, ‘Does edtech have a negative impact on learning?’ does not have a simple yes/no answer: sometimes it does, and sometimes it doesn’t.

“The question we need to be asking is, ‘when does edtech help learning?’ And the answer is, ‘it’s complicated’.”

title: AI cheating, leaked papers and marking errors: how exam protests went global
summary:
Student unrest sweeps India, Portugal and Mexico as grievances and pressure for good grades in tough job market collide

Families with teenagers in education know the private, hidden pain of exam season. But this year, what might have been a summer of quiet family anxiety has erupted in several countries into public unrest.

Exam-related turmoil has led to mass student protests in Mexico after nearly 60,000 university applicants were forced to resit tests amid suspected cheating, while Portugal’s disastrous attempt to digitise school exam marking sparked the country’s worst education crisis in decades.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Families with teenagers in education know the private, hidden pain of exam season. But this year, what might have been a summer of quiet family anxiety has erupted in several countries into public unrest.

Exam-related turmoil has led to mass student protests in Mexico after nearly 60,000 university applicants were forced to resit tests amid suspected cheating, while Portugal’s disastrous attempt to digitise school exam marking sparked the country’s worst education crisis in decades.

By far the largest and most ground-shaking incident was in India, however, where an exam paper leak affected millions of students and was linked to more than a dozen students taking their own lives. The scandal forced the education minister to resign, and challenged the government’s hold over its 1.4 billion citizens.

Why does this exam season seem to be particularly tense and volatile? Experts say the growth of AI cheating and attempts by academic institutions to digitise examinations are at the heart of the issue. When coupled with the high stakes of good grades in an increasingly precarious global economy, the result can be explosive.

“It would seem that exams are getting more fraught on a global scale,” said Dr Sarah Eaton of the Werklund School of Education at the University of Calgary. “The pressure on young people has absolutely changed.

“We’ve seen the economic situation change around the world in the last decade. And the results of one examination determining a person’s entire future really creates untenable pressure on young people,” said Eaton, a leading expert on academic ethics. “This is a tragedy when young people are dying by suicide because of an examination outcome.”

When a single test can determine a young person’s entire future, cheating is no longer just about individuals but becomes a systematic issue, said Eaton. This is compounded when illicit commercial industries, known as the “education mafia”, exploit student desperation by stealing and then selling exam papers, something that has become widespread in India and elsewhere.

Students from across India joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party, a youth-led protest campaign that began as an online satirical joke and grew into a nationwide outcry that poses an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.

“When you get large-scale fraud combined with systemic failure, there’s almost a guarantee of a breakdown of public trust,” said Eaton. “And once that trust is broken, it’s almost impossible to regain. I can’t imagine how India is going to deal with this, just given the levels of corruption and fraud that we’ve seen.”

In Portugal, the national fallout from a failed push by its education minister, Fernando Alexandre, to fully digitise the exam marking process has landed the government in a crisis. Parents, teachers, and students have been protesting, demanding Alexandre’s resignation after his policy resulted in serious marking errors.

Similar demonstrations took place in Mexico. The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam), the country’s most prestigious university, announced that due to abnormally high marks in entrance exam results, which raised suspicions of widespread cheating, approximately 58,000 students would have to retake the exam.

Schools worldwide are rushing to deal with AI use by students, either through bans or teaching AI literacy and ethics to pupils. Denmark announced this month that from the new term, teenagers would have to make a verbal defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating.

Eaton has implemented similar reforms in her class. “AI can generate a perfect essay in seconds. So an essay is no longer a viable way to demonstrate students’ learning,” she said. “We should let it die with dignity and find other ways to assess student learning.”

In Eaton’s view, cheating is a “human problem” and so grading and assessing student learning has historically also been a human responsibility, which she said cannot easily be off-loaded to the latest tech.

But what institutions around the world have been doing instead, she said, is hoping technology can be easily and cheaply used to prevent cheating en masse.

Dr Thomas Lancaster, a computer scientist at Imperial College London who researches the educational use of generative AI, has studied how cheating has gone hi-tech. It is no longer about sneaking notes written on a sleeve, he said, but sophisticated communication.

Lancaster says students have always cheated but it has become far easier, with pupils using earpieces or miniature cameras, and increasingly, communicating with friends or family with access to internet searches.

“I think the number of notes you sneak in, they’re only useful if they’re the right notes and if you can interpret them very quickly,” he said.

“But with any kind of communication technology, you can have that expertise waiting outside for you in a human form. They either know the answers; they’ve got the expertise; or they can look them up online. You can go further than that now and have access to AI to communicate directly during the exam as well,” he added. “It’s spy technology, really.”

Rather than individual student misconduct, Eaton said the failure to properly train educators was forcing students to spend valuable time trying to navigate through these “broken” systems rather than focusing on learning.

“This idea of these mass examinations happening at scale, it sort of dehumanises the learning process and the assessment process,” she said.

This, she said, “sort of perpetuates this idea that examinations are the most important thing for students. I think we’ve lost the thread. Learning should be the most important thing for students.”

title: The movement to remake school playgrounds as urban climate oases
summary:
Stepping into the schoolyard at the Adolph S. Ochs public school in Manhattan’s bustling Hell’s Kitchen neighborhood, you’re greeted by a canopy of trees. Painted sea turtles and birds adorn the pavement. Summer school kids run along the track encircling the green turf field, tossing balls back and forth. Other kids shoot hoops or decompress […]

The post The movement to remake school playgrounds as urban climate oases appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
Stepping into the schoolyard at the Adolph S. Ochs public school in Manhattan’s bustling Hell’s Kitchen neighborhood, you’re greeted by a canopy of trees. Painted sea turtles and birds adorn the pavement. Summer school kids run along the track encircling the green turf field, tossing balls back and forth. Other kids shoot hoops or decompress in the shade. After walking down nearby Ninth Avenue in the blistering heat, one finds it noticeably cooler here.

This schoolyard wasn’t always like this. Eleven years ago, it resembled many other city playgrounds: an open, unshaded expanse of black asphalt.

Now, it’s among 420 schoolyards across 26 states that the nonprofit Trust for Public Land says it is helping to transform from barren blacktop into welcoming oases for schoolchildren and local residents.

In late July, TPL hosted a two-day summit in New York City, bringing together school district leaders, landscape architects and environmental advocates from across the country to learn more about reinvigorating schoolyards. Keynote speakers extolled the benefits of nature-based play and keeping schoolyards open to the public when school isn’t in session.

A core part of TPL’s mission is ensuring that everyone in the country has access to a quality park within a 10-minute walk of their home.

Reinventing schoolyards starts with a thoughtfully rendered design. Students at a participating school survey classmates to learn more about their favorite park features and what their schoolyard really needs. From there, they work alongside landscape architects to help shape the design. Administrators, custodians, recess monitors and afterschool caretakers also take part.

“The users are the designers,” said Mary Alice Lee, who directs TPL’s NYC Playgrounds Program.

Designs include the classic staples — basketball hoops and jungle gyms — but reimagined: drab courts are repainted with colorful geometric designs. Structures include features inspired by natural elements, like artificial climbing boulders and tree stumps. Playful mosaics and murals grace building walls, giving life to once lackluster schoolyards.

But these designs aren’t driven just by aesthetics and opportunities for play. Climate change is exacerbating dangerous heat waves and increasing the frequency of downpours in some cities. Green-roofed gazebos and rain gardens to catch storm runoff can let schools help their neighborhoods mitigate difficult weather conditions.

At schoolyards such as the one at Adolph S. Ochs, asphalt playgrounds can worsen flooding and overwhelm the city’s drainage systems. Switching out blacktop for porous pavement allows rain to seep through rather than pool on the surface. A green gazebo roof, acting as a sponge, absorbs rainwater and reduces the flooding risk. On 90-degree days, unshaded asphalt surfaces can surpass 140 degrees, but shaded surfaces have been found to be at least 30 degrees cooler than those without protection from the sun.

TPL also wants these playgrounds to serve as vital community spaces outside of school hours, particularly in low-income areas that lack green spaces.

“When the school year is open to the community after hours, you’re fostering this great sense of care and sense of ownership,” said Danielle Denk, TPL’s community schoolyards initiative director. “There’s more people looking out for what happens there, and it just reinforces that positive use.”

New York City’s Schoolyards to Playgrounds program, a collaboration between city agencies and TPL, renovates public school yards and opens them to local neighborhoods outside of school hours. Other cities in the country also have shared use agreements — between two separate government entities, such as a school district and city — that allow the public to access schoolyards and other facilities outside of school hours. But because these agreements are not universal, access to safe, green spaces remains inconsistent across communities.

Close to 75 percent of U.S. residents who live in areas that have experienced the most nature loss are Black, Hispanic, Asian or Native American, according to an analysis by the Center for American Progress, a think tank.

These communities often bear the brunt of hazardous weather and experience worse health conditions. Research has linked proximity to tree canopies to lower cardiovascular disease and mortality rates.

Yet in cities like New York, green space is not distributed equitably.

Near Bayside, Queens, each resident has an average of more than 141 square feet of park space within a one-mile walk. But in Jackson Heights, Queens, which is majority Latino and Asian, the community has access to just 2 square feet per person.

At the summit, New York City councilmember Shekar Krishnan emphasized the need for community schoolyards within his Queens district, which includes Jackson Heights.

Schoolyards are “one of the few spaces we have — quite literally the only open spaces we have — where our children can play, and our community can come together,” said Krishnan. “It’s not that park space and green space is a luxury or privilege for some. It’s a right for all of us.”

Creating community schoolyards has its obstacles. Finding funding to start a project remains a challenge. TPL works with communities to obtain funding through public and private grants, but securing funds varies from city to city.

“The pros outweigh the cons, but we’re a cash-strapped city and district,” said Emma Melvin, green infrastructure program manager at the School District of Philadelphia.

Philadelphia has improved playgrounds with green infrastructure through nonprofit partnerships and grants, but covering long-term maintenance costs is challenging. Vandalism can also add to the expense, Melvin said.

“Sometimes a system can be easier to design but harder to maintain,” said Megan Garner, director of sustainability and green schools for the Philadelphia school district, during a summit workshop on building climate-resilient schoolyards.

As the summit drew to a close, rising ninth grader Nazarian Lopez spoke about being part of the process to redesign his schoolyard at MS 343 in the Bronx.

“Today, when I see teachers, staff, students and families using that space, I feel proud because I know something I helped imagine has become a part of everyday life,” he said.

Contact editor Caroline Preston at 212-870-8965, via Signal at CarolineP.83 or on email at preston@hechingerreport.org.

This story about playgrounds was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education. Sign up for Hechinger’s climate change newsletter.

title: Students don’t develop skills by accident – it takes work to make graduate attributes real
summary: Becky Hartnup explores how to close the gap between naming the skills students need and building them into the curriculum
full_text:
Few will disagree that graduates need to acquire or develop skills during their study. At a high level, there’s also a surprising degree of consensus on what sorts of skills are valuable; these tend to cluster around C words such as collaboration, creativity, communication, and critical thinking.

The arrival of AI hasn’t changed that; if anything, it’s only intensified the imperative to ensure graduates are able to demonstrate broad-based skills and apply them in industry.

As a consequence, graduate attributes frameworks, employability strategies, and skills agendas have become a fixture of institutional planning. The challenge is the gap between a strategy that names the skills students need and a curriculum that builds them. The issues are both conceptual and practical. Educators have to work out what it means, in disciplinary terms, to develop skills, and this approach is not well established in some subjects and disciplinary cultures. Then those involved in programme design need to identify opportunities for skills development within the curriculum, shape learning activities and resources to support that development, and assess students’ application of those skills in practice.

There’s no shortage of great models and frameworks, nor of individual enthusiasts who are championing innovation in their areas. But to scale and embed skills across an institution takes hard work and coordinated effort. A senior team can set a direction, but this only translates into a meaningful graduate attribute when it is designed into a module, taught by an academic who is confident in the approach and assessed in a way students recognise. Move too far top-down, and you will get a checklist list of attributes that no one owns. Rely purely on individual enthusiasts, and you will get pockets of brilliant practice that don’t translate across disciplinary contexts.

The Adobe Creative Campus network in the UK brings together multiple institutions with a shared aim: to realise strategic goals for student engagement and success through embedding use of Adobe tools in curricula. Beginning in 2020 with the first European Creative Campus, Teesside University, the network has grown to more than 20 institutions. As we’ve worked alongside colleagues who are seeking to make change happen, we keep hearing the same challenge: They want to develop their own distinctive approach, but they also want a cheat sheet with some use cases, examples, and ideas they can apply and build out from.

The context is pragmatic: when resources are tight, innovation can be amplified by good ideas from elsewhere, reconfigured for a different environment. And when you are asking faculty to change what they do, it’s essential to take account of the context in which most faculty are operating: high workloads, pressure on recruitment, and a fast-changing academic landscape, thanks to AI.

So to respond to this challenge, Adobe has been reflecting on the spaces between large-scale frameworks and individual practitioners, and the kinds of resources that can support the development of practice in that space. We’ve concluded that there needs to be a level of disciplinary focus and we’ve started with business schools, a context in which employability and value-add are always front and centre, and where the closeness to industry means that faculty are typically used to adapting curricula in light of business needs.

Aston’s power skills – lens, not leaflet

As a worked example, at Aston University, Deputy Dean Education: Student Experience and Success, Chris Umfreville is working through how the university’s Power Skills framework can be manifested and made authentic in curricula, working with the university’s careers and placements team. In a context where employability is part of the university’s heritage and founding mission, power skills are, in Chris’s words, a way of capturing a “vision for the idea of needing to prepare students for an ever-changing and uncertain future.”

The four power skills – AI and digital, innovation and entrepreneurship, inclusive leadership, and environmental sustainability – are intended to be “specific enough to have value but broad enough to allow for interpretation and application,” as Chris explains. All require a degree of technical knowledge and proficiency in addition to durable skills and the contextual awareness that employers value. But there is still plenty of room for interpretation and application within different disciplines.

Rather than either leaving that interpretation entirely up to individuals or enforcing a particular model, Aston has adopted a hybrid approach. Each of the power skills is designed as a five-hour stackable module, built with asynchronous online content using Adobe tools, and combining academic domain insight and industry expertise. But the deployment can vary. In some disciplines, where it makes sense to do so, a standalone power skills module as part of the overall programme. In others, power skills content is embedded within relevant modules, areas of study, or key moments in programmes.

For example, the business school chose to integrate the AI and digital module into Welcome Week. “That was a useful approach because it allowed us to showcase the VLE in ways that students would engage with, to wrap around an activity with students to allow for community and transition support, and at the same time to address the elephant in the room of AI use without terrifying the students or shouting at them about academic integrity,” says Chris. The session used generated AI images to demonstrate the benefits and limitations of AI, and highlight the need to apply a critical lens to written outputs.

During reading week, the school ran a voluntary environmental challenge, with students working in groups to create an environmental campaign (eg the promotion of green space in Birmingham) using Adobe tools, and working towards the award of an Adobe microcredential. The activity was designed to complement students completing the environmental sustainability Power Skill, providing an opportunity to apply the content in a local context, expanding their digital capabilities and gain recognition in the process.

While some staff are already attuned to these skills and how they show up in curricula, that is not true of everyone. “We don’t want to create more work for colleagues,” says Chris. “The module approach is useful, because we’re not asking all academic staff to be expert in these skills. Instead, we’re asking for identification of where there is alignment. You don’t need to understand everything Adobe does and teach it to students, for example, but we need you to know it exists and its potential uses, then be prepared to signpost to students and let them explore. That way, we can learn from them.”

From building the core content, the goal is to iterate and continue to embed and evolve until the Power Skills framework brings about the shift from short term strategic agenda to business as usual. The change this represents for student experience is subtle but significant. Aston was already strong on employability, but that work was, Chris says, “very output driven” and focused on CVs, self-presentation, and the procedural steps of applying for a job. Power skills content reframes the goal from performance to substance, with skills showing up as “a quality of you rather than something you perform.” It is a response to a real erosion, too. The durable skills students once absorbed through campus life and academic experience now develop less reliably, as part-time work, larger cohorts, and less time on campus eat into informal learning opportunities.

From practice to playbook

Aston is one case and one approach, but there are others across the Adobe Creative Campus network that we are useful to showcase and learn from. That’s the gap the Adobe business school guide, Driving Success in Business Schools, is designed to fill.

We quickly discarded broad-brush frameworks as too generic. Instead, we worked directly with specific institutions, auditing what they were doing. Some had leaders developing top-down approaches, and others had individual academics following their own curiosity. We were able to translate these authentic and specific use cases into broad frameworks that can support a wide range of other institutions.

UWE Bristol, was preparing to launch a new spine module for all 1000 students from across the business school. We explored how Adobe Express could support defined learning activities such as goal setting and planning, working with the digital team to create templates and with faculty to develop case studies. At Cardiff Metropolitan University, we worked from the bottom up, with highly engaged lecturers to create a hub for individual academics to showcase and share their ideas, building a “proof of concept” space that caught the attention of heads of department. And at Manchester Metropolitan University, we worked with course cohorts of different sizes to play-test activities like creating a living CV or switching from a presentation assessment to a multimedia pitch.

The guide includes all these case studies, along with templates to help you get started, Adobe Express Learning Kits to share with faculty, and inspiration for practical activities.

A key piece of learning from this exercise was that every stakeholder is essential in making change. Academics understand the students, the curriculum, and the workflows. Leadership provides strategy, permission, resources, and celebration. And the fuel that makes it all happen tends to be the digital learning and learning technology teams, who accelerate adoption by giving nervous academics safety nets and scaffolding to try something different.

In the past, we’ve seen that the gap between digital consumption and digital production hasn’t always been sufficiently visible, especially in pedagogy. Multimodal work asks us to think in different ways, engaging complex mental processes that synchronise image, text, and sound to make meaning. Just because you’ve seen a TV programme or listened to a podcast doesn’t mean you know how to make a good video or audio output and these complex communication approaches are becoming increasingly important in the workplace.

Digital poverty can combine with low academic confidence to discourage students from trying something if they’re not sure they will be successful. Yet getting comfortable with trying and failing is a key skill in itself. Across the board, the lecturers and digital learning teams I worked with were strong advocates for introducing these things in low-stakes, playful ways before they ever count towards an assessment, helping students take ownership of a project and build their confidence.

The guide won’t build anyone’s curriculum for them. But for institutions staring at the gap between a skills strategy and a lecture theatre, it offers something more useful than another framework: a map of the ideas, the stakeholders, and a springboard to turn ambition into practice.
